title: The impact of civil rights protests, 1960–74

review.note: Original content following 4HI1 Depth study 7, key topic 3.

learn.intro: In the 1960s sit-ins, Freedom Rides and mass marches forced the federal government to pass major civil rights laws. Later in the decade, frustration led many towards Black Power.

sections.title: 1. Sit-ins, Freedom Riders and the Meredith case

blocks.p: Sit-ins: on 1 February 1960 four black students sat at a whites-only lunch counter in Greensboro, North Carolina, and refused to leave. Sit-ins spread across the South, and many lunch counters desegregated. The Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC) was set up in April 1960.

Freedom Rides (1961): CORE sent black and white volunteers on buses through the South to test whether bus stations obeyed the law against segregation. At Anniston, Alabama, a bus was firebombed (May 1961); in Birmingham riders were beaten. The government eventually enforced desegregation of bus terminals.

Voting rights and the Meredith case: in 1962 James Meredith tried to enrol at the University of Mississippi. Riots broke out and two people were killed; President Kennedy sent federal marshals and troops, and Meredith graduated in 1963.

evidence: 1962: James Meredith at the University of Mississippi.

sections.title: 2. Martin Luther King's methods and campaigns

blocks.p: King believed in non-violent direct action: peaceful protest that would provoke a violent response from racists, which the media would show to the world, forcing the government to act.

Birmingham, Alabama (1963): police chief 'Bull' Connor used dogs and fire hoses on protesters, including children. Television pictures shocked the nation and President Kennedy proposed a civil rights bill.
The March on Washington (28 August 1963): about 250,000 people marched; King gave his 'I have a dream' speech, showing the movement's huge support.

Mississippi Freedom Summer (1964): volunteers registered black voters; three workers — James Chaney, Andrew Goodman and Michael Schwerner — were murdered. The Civil Rights Act (July 1964) banned segregation in public places and discrimination in jobs.
Selma (1965): marchers for voting rights were attacked by police on 'Bloody Sunday' (7 March). Shocked by the pictures, Congress passed the Voting Rights Act (August 1965), banning literacy tests.

sections.title: 3. The Nation of Islam, Malcolm X and Black Power

blocks.p: The Nation of Islam called for black separation, not integration. Its best-known speaker, Malcolm X, criticised King's non-violence and argued black people should defend themselves 'by any means necessary'. He left the Nation of Islam in 1964 and was assassinated in February 1965.

Reasons for Black Power: slow progress in the North, poverty in the ghettos, police brutality, and anger at the violence used against peaceful protesters. In 1966 Stokely Carmichael of SNCC popularised the slogan 'Black Power', meaning black pride and black control of black communities.

Race riots: in August 1965 riots in the Watts district of Los Angeles left 34 dead; more riots followed in other cities. The Black Panthers, founded in 1966 by Bobby Seale and Huey Newton, carried guns to monitor the police and ran community programmes such as free breakfasts for children.
1968 Olympics: in Mexico City, US athletes Tommie Smith and John Carlos raised black-gloved fists on the medal podium — a Black Power salute seen around the world.

flashcards.a: Many lunch counters desegregated; SNCC formed; young people drawn into the movement.
A Freedom Riders' bus was firebombed.

flashcards.q: How did King's non-violent methods work?
flashcards.a: Peaceful protest provoked violent responses, the media showed them, and the government was pressured to act.

flashcards.q: What did the Civil Rights Act 1964 do?
flashcards.a: Banned segregation in public places and discrimination in employment.

flashcards.q: Give three reasons for the growth of Black Power.
flashcards.a: Slow progress in the North; ghetto poverty; police brutality; Malcolm X's ideas; violence against peaceful protesters.

flashcards.q: What did the Black Panthers do?
flashcards.a: Armed patrols to watch the police; community programmes such as free breakfasts.
